content_en:
*Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross*

*Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. **To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level.** While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.*

## Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch *all bugs,* and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. *Formal verification* is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but *20* person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can *never* crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V<sup>1</sup> CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing *all* possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—*especially* those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

## Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the *specification* (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with *fuzz tests*. In these tests, developers write an *entry point*<sup>2</sup> into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the *fuzzer,* a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for *any* input less than 64 MB.<sup>3</sup> If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). # OpenAI lowers valuation target, raises up to $30 billion

**OpenAI is closing in on a new funding round of up to $30 billion but has lowered its valuation target to get there.** The company originally pitched investors on a $1.4 trillion valuation, according to internal documents obtained by the Financial Times. That number has since dropped to $1.25 trillion, CNBC also reports. The FT says demand was weaker than in previous rounds, with some backers experiencing "indigestion" after heavy investments in earlier fundraises.

UAE investors and investment firm Coatue are leading the $30 billion round. The funding is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI is also negotiating a commercial deal to secure additional compute capacity through the UAE, according to CNBC.

OpenAI confidentially filed an IPO prospectus with the SEC in June. CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that OpenAI would be a publicly traded company by 2027. CEO Sam Altman said in September that the timing was unfavorable for going public. He had already communicated that internally back in June. Competitor Anthropic is also preparing an IPO and is targeting a valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion.

# Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI

Uber announced the company-wide rollout of ChatGPT Work, an agent that helps employees take on a wide range of tasks within ChatGPT Enterprise, starting today. The rollout will make ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees across Uber’s global workforce.

Expanding from an initial pilot of 1,000 employees, the rollout will give teams across Uber access to an agentic platform designed to take on complex, multi-step tasks and deliver finished work. The expansion makes ChatGPT Work Uber’s first company-wide deployment of an agentic platform tailored for knowledge work.

ChatGPT Work connects with tools companies like Uber use on a daily basis, including Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack, enabling workers to research information, prepare meeting briefs, create presentations, analyze data and complete workflows across applications.

ChatGPT Work also gives Uber access to OpenAI’s portfolio of frontier models. Uber will benefit from models like GPT‑6.1 Sol which will be deployed as the default capability within ChatGPT Work, balancing frontier performance and cost efficiency. Uber teams will also be supported by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, including voice and image generation, giving them the flexibility to choose the right models and tools for different needs.

The rollout will be supported by Uber’s internal AI skills library, approved integrations and dedicated employee training, helping teams across functions including operations, finance, marketing and product put the technology to work. Uber’s developers and software engineering teams will also continue using Codex to accelerate software development and streamline coding workflows.

The expansion marks another step in Uber’s broader AI strategy and its collaboration with OpenAI. The companies plan to share further insights into adoption, use cases and measurable outcomes as the rollout progresses.

### Year-old AI research lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a reported $6B valuation

Artificial intelligence research lab Flapping Airplanes Inc. today announced it has raised $1 billion in new funding, about a year after it was founded.

Investors valued the startup at $6 billion in the deal, Bloomberg reported. No commercial product has come out of the lab yet.

Flapping Airplanes is trying to build AI models that learn from far less data than today’s frontier systems consume. Most of its first year went into new primitives for graphics processing units. That work, according to the company’s announcement on X, enables new algorithms that could “dramatically reshape AI’s cost structure.”

The founders have built what they describe as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework.” Index Ventures Management’s post on the round says a megakernel runs an entire program on a GPU as a single kernel, so the chip stops losing time between steps. Flapping Airplanes says its framework can handle a full training run, serve inference and play a video game at the same time inside one kernel. Memory-bound inference can then overlap with compute-bound training on the same chip.

“A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” co-founder Asher Spector told TechCrunch. Spector holds a statistics doctorate from Stanford University.

His brother Ben Spector, the chief executive, started the student-run startup accelerator Prod while at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and is now a computer science doctoral student at Stanford. In 2024 he was lead author on ThunderKittens, an open-source toolkit for writing fast GPU kernels. Aidan Smith, the third co-founder and a Thiel Fellow, worked at Neuralink Corp. during college. Index describes a team of a couple dozen people working in person in San Francisco.

Index and Lux Capital Management co-led the Series A round. Mark Xu of Index is joining the board. Sequoia Capital Operations and GV Management Co. joined Index in the $180 million seed round in January, and both returned for this one. Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, Valor Equity Partners LP, Atreides Management LP, Jump Trading Group, XTX Ventures and Nvidia Corp. also appear on the list of institutional backers the company posted on X.

Xu and Shardul Shah, also of Index, argued that demand for AI will keep outrunning the supply of compute and data. Robotics, trading and life sciences were the markets they singled out as needing more efficient AI.

By Bloomberg’s count, the valuation has roughly quadrupled in the nine months since the seed round. Investors have now put $1.18 billion into the company.

content_en:
Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.

The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done.

The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million.

Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday.

Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America.

content_en:
I spent two days touring Intel’s most advanced fab and talking to its technical leadership to understand what the chips of the future will look like.

A lot of what’s coming next – gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, hybrid bonding – is hard to follow without actually seeing it, so we made all the awesome animated explainers that I wish I had while I was prepping.

I also asked Intel’s leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous shock in demand from AI.

AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel’s CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today’s global stock of chipmaking tools.

What kinds of tricks can foundries pull to extend this crossover point where demand surges way ahead of supply?

This was a totally new format for us - hope you enjoy!

I also made flashcards for the concepts I had to learn to prep for this episode here.

Watch on YouTube, Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

- WorkOS helps you do business with enterprises. It gives you access to all the features most commonly required by enterprises: SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more. It’s easy to plug these features in — it only takes a few lines of code — and WorkOS is releasing new functionality all the time, including things like auth for agents. If you want to join the 3,000+ companies that rely on WorkOS, go to workos.com

- Jane Street built a powerful tool called magic-trace to help analyze and debug their trading systems. It only exists because one engineer noticed a feature on Intel chips called Processor Trace and thought it’d be valuable to build on top of. Now, traders and developers across Jane Street use magic-trace every single day! If you want to be trusted to pursue the ideas you think matter most, Jane Street is hiring. Go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh

- Antithesis’ testing platform lets you perfectly reproduce every single bug you find. That’s because it runs on a fully deterministic computer, which strips out all the unpredictability that can make certain bugs flaky and hard to pin down. To build it, Antithesis found every source of non-determinism in Intel’s x86 architecture and either sealed it off or replaced it with a controlled simulation. Learn more at antithesis.com/dwarkesh

### 00:00:00 – The AI demand shock

**Dwarkesh Patel**

There’s never been as big a shock to the semiconductor industry as the current surge in demand from AI.

**Gary Dickerson**

**Peter Wennink**

*Easily 40-50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.*

**Dwarkesh Patel**

Progress in AI has been driven by exponentially increasing compute. To sustain that progress, foundries like Intel will need to manufacture far more leading-edge compute, both by producing more chips and by improving what each chip can do.

But the production of these chips is bottlenecked by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers. Most famously, ASML’s EUV machines.

I’m joined by Chris Auth, who leads development of all the processes that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens. If 14A is going to come out in three years or two years from now, what is happening from now till then?

I want you to walk me through as much detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the yield improving?” to what kind of telemetry you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run? I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.

**Chris Auth**

14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage, so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now. Right now, we’re getting very close to where we’re finalizing the process. We’re finalizing the tool sets that it will be manufactured on, and we’re working on the fine-tuning of each of the process steps.

There are about 2,000 steps in the factory that you have to go do. You need to do really intricate work at each one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned, it can go into manufacturing, it can run thousands of wafers a week on this process, and it can be repeatable every single time.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

**Chris Auth**

We have tools that will look at the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.” Then also at the end of line, either electrical test or we sort and see where the fails are. We will identify failures, and then we will get analysis on those failures. We’ll cross-section it.

You were in the TEM lab yesterday, and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect, and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh, that defect is between these layers, so it must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section, which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”

What we’ve learned is that you don’t want to do too much innovation in one node, because the more innovation that you do, the more complex it becomes.

While you’ll be able to get that to work, you need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece. # Anthropic's Claude now writes code and proves it safe automatically

## Key Points

- Anthropic and partner Theorem used Claude to mathematically verify existing software code and generate formal proofs of its correctness.
- The model produced roughly 180 million lines of proof code for 123 open-source libraries in just a few weeks. Along the way, Claude caught hundreds of bugs that conventional testing had missed.
- If AI can write code and prove it's correct, software automation might take a major leap. Anthropic wants formal verification with AI to become as routine as standard testing.

**Anthropic used Claude to mathematically prove that existing code is correct. The approach tackles a core problem with AI-generated software but comes with strict practical limits.**

Proving that software runs error-free under all circumstances has always been prohibitively expensive. A team of specialists needed 20 person-years just to formally verify the small operating system kernel seL4, so the method was reserved for extreme cases like Airbus avionics software.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with partner Theorem, let Claude take over the proof work instead. The model produced roughly 180 million lines of mathematical proof code in just a few weeks, drawing on test programs from 123 open-source libraries in Google's OSS-Fuzz security project.

Rather than writing new code, Claude verified existing software by translating crash tests into mathematical problems, analyzing the compiled machine code, and producing extensive proofs. An independent verification program called Rocq automatically checks those proofs, and according to Anthropic, the process needs almost no human reviewers. The researchers call it "fully autonomous" proof generation, though the tools and formal foundations were built by humans at Theorem.

## Claude catches bugs that years of testing missed

While generating proofs, Claude ran into hundreds of bugs and was allowed to fix them itself. Many would have slipped past conventional testing because they only show up under very specific conditions, like unusually large input files or a particular sequence of accesses, the researchers say.

During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, for example, the team found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported for that software in an entire year. In another application, Claude caught a logical error that had gone undetected for over a decade. Even when a complete proof ultimately fails, Anthropic says, the attempt still surfaces real bugs.

## What formal verification can and can't do

Anthropic acknowledges that "formally verified" doesn't mean "error-free." The proofs only hold under strict conditions: a specific processor architecture, single-threaded programs, and inputs under 64 MB. In practice, these libraries run on different hardware and in different configurations.

The compute cost is steep, with individual proofs running up hundreds of millions of tokens. Anthropic doesn't report total project costs. But if AI can verify its own code, developers can trust AI-generated software more and spend less time reviewing it. That saves costs not just on verification but on the entire coding process. A smaller test run also showed that proofs are reusable, and newer models are getting more efficient: Opus 5.5 solves half the proofs with about 40 percent fewer tokens than Opus 5.

The project strengthens the case for software automation. If AI can write code and guarantee its correctness under defined conditions, the question shifts from "Can AI program?" to "Can AI prove that the code it writes is safe?" If the answer is yes, the consequences could go well beyond today's coding tools.

Case in point: Anthropic expects formal verification with AI will soon become as practical as standard testing, and Theorem's roadmap already targets critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
excerpt: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that's working to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems.
title_en: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
excerpt_en: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that's working to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems.
content_en:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

### Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

### Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

### What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
excerpt: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
title_en: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
excerpt_en: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
content_en:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint, on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video, it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference.

Clarifying the technical details, Socher tweeted that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

title: On the ground at Nvidia's AI showpiece: Jensen-mania, robot ducks and neocloud distress
excerpt: The word on the ground from Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin.
title_en: On the ground at Nvidia's AI showpiece: Jensen-mania, robot ducks and neocloud distress
excerpt_en: The word on the ground from Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin.
content_en:
*This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.*

Jensen Huang has been busy.

Nvidia's GTC in Berlin was the grand finale of a week-and-a-half whistle stop European tour. Huang met with world leaders — including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — announced new products and even spent time talking to small robot ducks on stage.

The Nvidia chief must be tired. At a media Q&A on Thursday morning, he gave reporters an insight into his mantra. Talking about bringing data centers online faster, Huang said: "Try less sleep, which is what I do."

And the trip's not over for Huang. Today, he's in Kazakhstan, touting the country's potential as a major AI hub.

Amid all the activity in Germany, I spent two days in Berlin running around meeting with neocloud execs, investors and data center builders and suppliers.

Here are the main themes that came up.

## Neocloud distress

The final day of the conference came amid a selloff among public neocloud stocks. CoreWeave ended the day down 10% and Nebius dropped 7% by market close.

It continued a tumultuous period for companies leasing AI compute, with many of their stocks plummeting on concerns over heavy borrowing.

Huang — perhaps unsurprisingly considering Nvidia's sizeable stakes in many of those companies — was more bullish.

"If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts," Huang told CNBC.

Despite that, there was concern about the neocloud sector among many of the folk I spoke to at GTC. The "magnitude of businesses with no credit rating" was "freaking the market out," said one exec at an AI infrastructure company I met with.

## Data centers are getting smaller

Speaking onstage in Berlin, Huang announced a new product that packs seven of Nvidia's Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container and is designed to be transported on normal roads.

It's a play to get AI compute online more quickly amid huge demand. Huang told the audience that billions of dollars in revenue can be lost by delays in getting data centers up and running.

"By moving this into the supply chain, the speed by which we can turn on" will ramp up, he said.

Major compute consumers are already exploring opportunities for smaller data center deployments. Sources had told me in September that OpenAI and Anthropic have been hunting for smaller AI data center deals.

## Capital could be the next big bottleneck

AI infrastructure is hugely expensive to build.

Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.

A 1 gigawatt data center costs about $50 billion, Huang told the Berlin audience on Wednesday.

"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," he said during his CNBC interview on Thursday.

"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," he told my colleague Arjun Kharpal, though the CEO added: "That's going to get solved."

One person I spoke to on the sidelines, an exec at an AI infrastructure financing company, said "very soon capital will become the bottleneck."

## News edit

**OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation** led by UAE investors.

**Musk said Tesla and SpaceX formed special committees to discuss merger,** on an earnings call this week.

**Trump said data centers should pay communities a 'dividend' to win support,** amid public backlash about the facilities.

**OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring** — and one lied about it.

**The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek** from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.

## One more thing

Yesterday, my colleagues Annie Palmer and Lora Kolodny dug into the accelerating demand for alternative satellite internet services, amid Ukraine's problems with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield.

But, as they write, few alternatives to the company's systems exist and other options are not yet comparable.

content_en:
**Cognitive Credit**, the London-based provider of corporate credit data, analytics and AI technology, has secured a €35.73 million ($40 million) strategic growth investment.

The investment round was led by global growth equity firm Summit Partners, with continued participation from existing investor ETFS Capital. The investment follows an €8.93 million ($10 million) Series B led by ETFS Capital in September 2024, and a €7.17 million (£6 million) Series A led by Fitch Ventures in November 2021

“*High-quality data at speed and scale is critical to powering AI workflows that credit professionals will increasingly rely on for high-stakes decisions*,” said **Chris Bon**, a Partner at Summit Partners who has joined the Cognitive Credit Board of Directors.

Founded in 2017 by Robert Slater, Cognitive Credit was built by ex-credit analysts who experienced first-hand the limitations of relying on tools designed for equity markets, at a time when no credible alternative existed for the credit space. The company set out to address what it saw as a long-overdue digital transformation in corporate credit markets, one of the world’s largest asset classes with nearly €12.5 trillion ($14 trillion) raised in 2025 alone, according to OECD’s Global Debt Report 2026.

Cognitive Credit’s integrated web application provides support across the credit research workflow, combining verified data, advanced analytics and domain-specialist generative AI capabilities. Its platform is powered by proprietary data developed through the analysis of hundreds of thousands of financial reports to give analysts on-demand access to audit-grade credit models and primary reporting libraries across 3,500+ corporate bond and loan issuers in the US, Europe and emerging markets.

“*Cognitive Credit is purpose-built for credit analysis and leverages institutional-grade technology to provide speed, precision, and auditability across thousands of issuers and to support leading banks and asset managers in use cases where accuracy and verifiability are critical. We’re excited to partner with Robert and the team as they further expand their presence and offering and help credit professionals put AI to work with confidence*,” added Bon.

Cognitive Credit’s product suite includes a web application, an Excel add-in that streams proprietary financials directly into existing spreadsheets, a REST API for integration into institutional tech stacks, and a Claude Connector that allows analysts to query issuers and surface financial insights directly from within the Claude environment.

The company says all the outputs are fully auditable and traceable to source, a critical differentiator for institutional clients. This emphasis on verified data could be the reason why the company has managed to power analytical workflows for more than 80% of the top 25 global asset managers by AUM and all top 10 global debt league table investment banks. In a statement, Summit Partners says Cognitive Credit has achieved 240% active user growth and more than doubled its global bond and loan issuer coverage.

“*Demand for credit-specialist technology will continue to accelerate from here, and we are pleased to partner with Summit Partners on our next phase of growth. With the imminent launch of DealConnect, ongoing innovation in our AI deployments, and many additional capabilities planned for 2027, we’re offering credit teams the highest quality data and analytics they require for differentiated analysis and high impact decision-making*,” said **Slater**, founder and CEO of Cognitive Credit.

With this strategic investment, Cognitive Credit will accelerate its commercial expansion into the US and advance its next generation of products. These include the imminent launch of DealConnect, designed to enable on-demand access to detailed credit models for private issuers that report via secure data rooms, and the pending deployment of agentic credit analysis. The company also plans to continue expanding its issuer coverage into new credit markets.

### OpenAI to make its most advanced AI models available in Google Cloud

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to make its latest large language models accessible in Google Cloud.

The LLMs will be available through the Alphabet Inc.’s unit Model Garden service. It provides access to more than 200 neural networks from Google, its partners and the open-source ecosystem. The lineup includes not only LLMs but also smaller, more specialized models optimized for tasks such as translation.

The first LLM OpenAI is bringing to Google Cloud is its flagship GPT-6 Astra model. The algorithm is responsible for several of the AI-produced math discoveries that the company has published in recent weeks. It also achieved a perfect score on ExploitBench, a benchmark that measures LLMs’ ability to find and exploit cybersecurity flaws.

Astra includes safety optimizations designed to make it suitable for enterprise use. According to OpenAI, the model causes “fewer misaligned outcomes” than all the other frontier models it has evaluated. It’s configured not to bypass user-defined restrictions on the tasks that it can perform.

Google Cloud customers will also receive access to GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, two scaled-down versions of Astra that OpenAI launched in late September. They trade off some output quality for a significant reduction in token pricing. Sol and Luna cost five and 100 times less than Astra, respectively.

“We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs,” said Google Cloud Chief Executive Thomas Kurian.

Cloud providers offer discounts to enterprises that sign long-term spending commitments. OpenAI says that Google Cloud customers can use those commitments to pay for access to its models. That removes the need for users to set up a new AI budget, which eases procurement.

Astra, Sol and Luna will become generally available in Google’s Model Garden within a few weeks. The companies plan to follow up the launch by bringing the models to the search giant’s Confidential Compute portfolio of infrastructure services.

Server-grade central processing units such as those Google uses include a security feature called TEE. The technology can encrypt a segment of the host server’s memory in a manner that only makes it accessible to a specific workload. Google’s Confidential Compute services use the technology to secure customer workloads. Additionally, they can ease use cases such as sharing a dataset among multiple organizations for AI training purposes.

OpenAI also plans to make its models available via Google’s Antigravity and Gemini Agent products. Antigravity is a vibe coding tool that uses agent ensembles to speed up software projects. Gemini Agent, in turn, is designed to automate business tasks that span multiple cloud applications.

title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
excerpt: The social media giant is planning a new stock strategy to help power its broad investments in AI models and services.
title_en: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
excerpt_en: The social media giant is planning a new stock strategy to help power its broad investments in AI models and services.
content_en:
Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose, however, by 68% year-over-year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

content_en:
### Nvidia turns the AI factory into a product, and agents into the workload

For most of the past half-decade, the narrative around Nvidia Corp. has largely centered on the graphics processing unit. The questions have been who has allocation, how much faster the next generation is and whether anyone can close the gap.

At GTC Berlin early today, Chief Executive Jensen Huang spent surprisingly little of his keynote on silicon. Instead, he argued that artificial intelligence constraints have shifted to deployment speed, power, security, and the ability to put enterprise data to work, and that Nvidia intends to have an answer for each. “We were early to observe that, in fact, AI is a manufacturing industry,” Huang told the audience. “Rather than a tool that’s used by us, it is now part of machinery, an infrastructure, factories that are producing intelligence.”

Those comments from Huang tie together most of the massive news payload from Berlin. A summary of the news includes Nvidia introducing DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners in containers; launching the OpenShell Reference Architecture to run agents safely; expanding its Agent Toolkit with an Agent Knowledge Foundation and a new family of structured-data models called Kumo; and deepening its push into telecom with Nokia and European operators.

Individually, these are product launches. Together, they show Nvidia moving from selling the most important component in AI to selling the operating model for AI.

### Time to first token is the new metric

One of the more interesting moments in the keynote came when Huang did back-of-the-envelope math on stage. A 1-gigawatt AI factory costs about $50 billion and should generate roughly $40 billion in annual revenue. Delay it by a quarter, and about $10 billion in revenue is lost. “$10 billion worth of revenue will make anybody anxious,” he said.

That’s an interesting and correct way to think about AI infrastructure economics. The cost that keeps AI builders up at night is no longer the price of hardware; it’s the cost of hardware sitting idle while crews pull cable. A modern AI build is a construction project, with kilometers of copper and fiber assembled on site by scarce, specialized labor, especially in Europe.

DSX POD embeds that work into the factory and hides the complexity from the customer. Each pod holds seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, with roughly 20 kilometers of NVLink copper and 17 kilometers of scale-out networking, all cabled, plumbed, and tested before shipment. Nvidia says that deployment at a prepared site drops from six months to as little as 14 days.

The more interesting question is where this fits. DSX POD won’t replace gigawatt campuses, which still benefit from economies of scale. The sweet spot is the hundreds-of-megawatts tier, where an operator has a site and power but lacks the time or permitting runway for a full land, power, and shell build. That’s exactly where Europe’s neoclouds, sovereign AI projects and telcos operate. The 14-day figure assumes the site is ready, with delivery set for early 2027. Containers compress integration, but they don’t fix grid interconnect queues. DSX POD shifts the long pole in the tent; it doesn’t remove it.

### Power is now a design input

The DSX platform beneath the pod is where Nvidia does some of its most important engineering work, which tends to fly under the radar. Warm-water, closed-loop cooling lets operators in suitable climates skip evaporative towers, which Nvidia estimates saves 54 million liters of water per day at 2 gigawatts. DSX MaxLPS directs power to where workloads need it, and Nvidia says this delivers the same output with up to 30% less power.

The piece I’d watch most closely is DSX Flex. During the Euro 2020 match between England and Germany, millions of Britons put the kettle on at halftime, and the grid saw roughly a one-gigawatt spike. Today, when a grid operator needs a data center to back off, the process is mostly manual, often a phone call. DSX Flex automates that interaction, allowing AI factories to defer or throttle work and return capacity.

That matters because data centers that behave like flexible loads are easier to connect and more readily accepted by communities. The industry must stop treating data centers purely as consumers on the grid and start treating them as partners to grid operators. Hyperscalers are already moving in this direction; the difference is that Nvidia is trying to make it a standard.

### Agent security belongs in the infrastructure

The second half of the keynote shifted from the factory to what runs inside it, increasingly agents rather than models. Huang described an agent as consisting of five parts: the model, the harness, the sandbox, knowledge and tools. He was clear about the priority. “The agent is an autonomous system that has access to files, resources and networks, as well as tools, and we need to make sure that the privileges we provide this autonomous system are minimal and that we constantly monitor it,” he said.

Much of the AI safety debate has centered on model alignment and guardrails, assuming a well-behaved model is enough. It isn’t. No model can be trained to understand the policy requirements of every business and regulated industry. Agents are probabilistic systems that will find creative ways to solve problems, and some of those approaches will touch data or take actions no one intended. They need deterministic controls enforced outside their reach.

That’s the thesis behind the OpenShell Reference Architecture. Harnesses run on Vera CPUs, models run on Vera Rubin, and BlueField-4 with Nvidia Sentry runs as an isolated monitor between them, capable of cutting off an agent in milliseconds. Network professionals will recognize the pattern. That’s why the industry moved away from host-based security alone and shifted enforcement into the network. It also lets security teams author policies for their own country and industry, which is especially important in Europe.

As expected, the ecosystem response to align with Nvidia has been strong, with CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., Palo Alto Networks Inc., Zscaler Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and others adding support. The question is whether OpenShell, which is open source and runs on x86 or Arm, can provide hardware-isolated enforcement without BlueField. Enterprises should distinguish the protections available through OpenShell software from the additional hardware enforcement provided by BlueField-4 and Sentry.

### Knowledge is where agents earn their keep

“What turns these agents into super agents is giving them access to your company’s knowledge,” Huang said. Enterprises hold an estimated 70% of the world’s data, and most of it hasn’t been prepared for agents. The industry’s attention has focused mostly on documents and PDFs, yet much of the business value lies in the rows and columns of enterprise resource planning, supply chain and financial systems, and language models aren’t built to reason over that data.

Historically, getting a prediction from a table meant building a custom model for a single question. Kumo is a family of predictive models that can answer many “what-if” questions against the same data. That’s the kind of capability that turns agents from chat interfaces into operational tools.

It also debunks the ridiculous “AI will kill software” narrative. “Some people said that AI is going to be the end of software, the end of tools companies,” Huang said. “It’s exactly the opposite.” I agree. Agents need simulators, solvers and databases, and the companies that own those tools become more valuable when they package them for agents.

Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers.

The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely. Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others.

Now it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart president and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club.

It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user.

What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent.

The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do.

With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set.

The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending.

The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary.

Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent.

Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site.

title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
title_en: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
content_en:
# NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required

## TL;DR

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native `structured-data-models` and `kumo-engine` libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM.

- **Paper:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
- **Model Code:** https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
- **Model Weights:** https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational
- **Client Code:** https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client
- **NIM Documentation:** https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

## The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models

Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.

The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:

**Better accuracy today:** As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.

**Simplicity and agility:** One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.

**Agents that can predict:** LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.

Today, we are introducing **Kumo Relational** (Paper, GitHub, HuggingFace), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.

## How Kumo Relational Works

Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (*e.g.*, "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.

Kumo Relational is a *Relational Foundation Model* that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through *in-context learning* by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (*e.g.*, "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

*Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.*

To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: **(1)** understand the values within each table, **(2)** relate records across tables, and **(3)** relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

*Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.*

**Automatic Context Generation:** Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.

**Reasoning Within Tables:** A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.

**Reasoning Across Tables:** A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.

## How Kumo Relational Was Built

Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.

The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.

Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations.

## Performance

In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning

title: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
excerpt: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
title_en: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
excerpt_en: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
content_en:
The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation.

PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites. It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.

The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.

Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.

Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post. Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.

Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.

Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)

OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.

In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.

Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

### Red Hat and Nvidia expand their partnership to secure autonomous AI agents

Red Hat Inc. today expanded its collaboration with Nvidia Corp. to help enterprises secure autonomous artificial intelligence agents, govern access to AI models and deploy workloads on Nvidia’s upcoming Vera Rubin data center infrastructure.

Announced at Nvidia’s GTC event in Berlin, the updates center on Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia, combining agent runtime controls, model inference software and hardware support across hybrid cloud environments. Red Hat also said it’s working to integrate Nvidia’s OpenShell Reference Architecture into its AI platforms as a native capability.

The security approach addresses two risks: agents exceeding their authorized boundaries and attackers compromising agents through techniques such as prompt injection or supply chain attacks. The companies aim to place security controls outside the agent and, where appropriate, the host operating system as well.

“An agent shouldn’t enforce its own boundaries,” John Fanelli, vice president of enterprise software at Nvidia, said in a statement. “Those controls belong outside the agent, in the runtime and the infrastructure beneath it.”

OpenShell provides a sandbox runtime for agents. Beneath that software layer, Nvidia’s Sentry security framework runs on the company’s BlueField data processing units, using its DOCA Argus software to monitor workloads from a separate hardware security domain.

In an accompanying technical blog, Red Hat said Argus inspects selected host memory structures to observe processes, files and network activity without requiring monitoring software on the host. An integrated security system can use its alerts to trigger BlueField policies that isolate an affected workload.

The architecture builds on existing BlueField-3 support in Red Hat OpenShift 4.22. It separates AI workloads running on server CPUs from networking and security services running on BlueField’s Arm processors. When configured to restrict host access, that separation helps protect infrastructure controls even if an attacker compromises the host.

Red Hat says Sentry can quarantine a compromised agent in milliseconds. Moving monitoring and networking functions onto the data processing unit also reduces demands on host CPUs, leaving more capacity for AI workloads.

### Model controls

The partnership also addresses the model infrastructure agents need to reason and act. A joint reference design combines Model-as-a-Service access controls and an AI Gateway with inference technologies including vLLM, llm-d, Nvidia Dynamo and Nvidia NIM microservices.

Based on Nvidia’s Inference Hub reference design, it supports self-service model discovery, access policies, rate limits and subscription entitlement tracking. Separating access governance from model execution is intended to help enterprises manage quotas, attribute costs and maintain performance across hybrid environments.

The companies also announced joint support for Nvidia Nemotron models, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, in the vLLM inference and serving engine and Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia. Red Hat highlighted quantization and speculative decoding techniques intended to reduce inference latency while preserving accuracy.

For hardware deployment, Red Hat said its Enterprise Linux for Nvidia now supports Vera CPUs and is prepared for the Vera Rubin platform. The companies are targeting operating system and platform compatibility when the new hardware becomes available.

An accompanying operating system blog explained that RHEL for Nvidia 26.03 modifies a limited set of core packages to accommodate new hardware while retaining standard RHEL userspace and security controls, including Security-Enhanced Linux. Users can transition to mainline RHEL without reinstalling once the hardware patches mature and enter the upstream Linux kernel.

Red Hat said the joint use cases, reference designs and agent capabilities are available through partners including Cisco Systems Inc., Dell Technologies Inc. and Lenovo Group Ltd., while work continues on native OpenShell integration.
